intro: Who made your lunch? Who made your shoes? Many people worked to make them. In this unit, you meet the workers and makers.
You will follow bread from a farm to your table. Then your class will hold a market day. You will buy, sell and count money.
By the end, you can tell a producer from a consumer. You can explain what a market is. You can say why prices go up or down.
bigQuestion: How do workers, makers and buyers help each other get what they need?

timeline.t: A farmer plants wheat seeds in a field.
A truck carries the wheat to the mill.
The mill grinds the wheat into flour.
A baker bakes bread, and a store sells it.
Your family buys the bread. You are a consumer.
Room 12 makes bookmarks and cards to sell.
Market day: buyers and sellers meet and trade.
The class counts the money and plans next time.

words.d: a person who makes goods or gives a service
a person who buys or uses goods and services
things people make that you can touch, like bread or shoes
a job one person does to help another, like a haircut
a place where buyers and sellers meet to trade
a person who pays money to get something
a person who gives something in trade for money
how much money you pay to buy something

test.q: A farmer grows corn. What is the farmer?
test.why: The farmer makes a good, so the farmer is a producer.
A shoe is a thing you can touch. That makes it a good.

test.q: You drink milk. What are you?
test.why: You use the milk, so you are a consumer.
A mill grinds wheat into flour.

test.q: Why is a truck driver important for bread?
choices: The driver eats all of it
test.why: Moving goods is transportation. It gets bread to the store.

choices: A place where buyers and sellers meet
test.why: Buyers and sellers meet at a market to trade.

test.q: Nobody buys the paper flowers. What might happen?
test.why: When nothing sells, a seller may lower the price.

test.q: Three bookmarks cost 10 cents each (example). How much for all three?
Everyone wants the cards. What can happen?
test.why: When many buyers want something, it can sell out.

test.q: Which rule makes a market fair?
test.why: Honest signs help buyers trust sellers.

write.prompt: Plan a table for market day. What will you make? What price will you pick (a class example)? What will you do if nobody buys? Draw or tell your plan.
tips: Say what product you will make.
Name the resources you need, like paper and markers.
Write your price on a sign. Keep it honest.
Tell what you will do if it does not sell, or if it sells out.

title: Workers, Makers and Markets

chapters.title: From Farm to Table
chapters.bigQuestion: How many people help bring one loaf of bread to your table?

story.title: One Loaf, Six Helpers
story.kicker: A loaf of bread passes through many hands before you eat it.
paragraphs: Maya ate a slice of toast. She asked her dad a question. "Where does bread come from?" Dad smiled. "Let us follow it back," he said.
First, a farmer planted wheat seeds. The wheat grew tall and gold. The farmer cut it down. A truck driver took the wheat to a mill.
At the mill, a miller ground the wheat. It turned into soft flour. A baker mixed the flour with water and yeast. The bread baked in a hot oven.
A driver took the bread to the store. A clerk put it on the shelf. Dad bought it. Then Maya ate it. Six people helped make her toast!
story.think: Who was the most important helper in Maya's bread story? Can the bread get to her without any one of them?

lessons.title: Producers Make Things
lessons.mainIdea: A producer makes a good or gives a service.
reading: A baker makes bread. A farmer grows corn. A person who makes things is a *producer*. The bread and corn are *goods*. Goods are things you can touch.
Some producers do not make things. A doctor helps you feel better. A bus driver gives you a ride. A helpful job like that is a *service*.
So a producer can make a good. A producer can give a service. Both are work that helps people.

words.d: a person who makes goods or gives a service
things people make that you can touch, like bread or shoes
a job one person does to help another, like a haircut

look.title: The Busy Street
look.text: Look down a busy street. A baker pulls hot rolls from an oven. A barber cuts a man's hair. A woman sells red apples from a cart.
look.prompt: Which helper gives a service? Which helpers sell goods?

check.q: A baker makes bread. What is the baker?
check.why: The baker makes something, so the baker is a producer.

check.q: Which one is a service?
check.why: A haircut is a job someone does for you. Shoes and bread are goods you can touch.

check.q: Which one is a good?
check.why: Crayons are things you can touch, so they are goods.

lessons.title: Consumers Use Things
lessons.mainIdea: A consumer buys or uses goods and services.
reading: Maya eats toast. She is using a good. A person who buys or uses goods and services is a *consumer*.
You are a consumer every day. You eat lunch. You ride the bus. You wear shoes. Other people made these things for you.
Producers make things. Consumers use them. Producers need consumers. Consumers need producers too.

words.d: a person who buys or uses goods and services

look.title: Breakfast Time
look.text: Picture your breakfast table. There is a bowl of cereal. There is a cup of milk. There is a banana. You eat it all up.
look.prompt: Who is the consumer at this table? Name one producer who helped.

check.q: Maya eats a banana. What is Maya?
check.why: Maya uses the banana, so she is a consumer.

check.q: Why do producers need consumers?
choices: Consumers buy and use what they make
check.why: Producers make things for people to use. Consumers are those people.

check.q: You ride the school bus. What are you using?
check.why: The bus driver gives you a ride. A ride is a service.

lessons.title: Farmer, Mill and Bakery
lessons.mainIdea: Bread is made in steps, and each step has a worker.
reading: Bread starts on a farm. A farmer plants wheat. The wheat grows all summer. Then the farmer cuts it. This is the first step.
Next, the wheat goes to a *mill*. The mill grinds the wheat into flour. Then a baker mixes flour, water and yeast. The baker bakes the bread.
Farm, then mill, then bakery. Each step needs the step before it. No wheat means no flour. No flour means no bread.

words.d: a place with machines that grind wheat into flour
a soft powder made from ground wheat, used to bake bread

look.title: Steps to Make Bread
look.prompt: What step comes right after the farmer grows wheat?

check.q: What does a mill make from wheat?
check.why: A mill grinds wheat into flour.

check.q: What comes first in making bread?
check.why: Without wheat from the farm, there is nothing to grind or bake.

check.q: The mill is closed. What happens?
check.why: Each step needs the one before it. No mill means no flour for the baker.

lessons.title: Trucks, Trains and Stores
lessons.mainIdea: Trucks and trains carry goods, and stores sell them.
reading: Wheat does not walk to the mill! A truck or a train carries it. Bread rides in a truck to the store. Moving goods is called *transportation*.
At the store, a clerk puts the bread on a shelf. The store sells the bread to families. A *store* is a place where people buy goods.
Drivers and clerks are workers too. They do not make the bread. But they help it get to you.

words.d: moving people or goods from one place to another
a place where people buy goods

look.title: The Long Train
look.text: Look at a long train by a farm field. It has many cars. The cars are full of grain. The train rolls away to a far city.
look.prompt: Why do farmers need trains and trucks?

check.q: How does bread get to the store?
check.why: Trucks carry goods from the bakery to the store. That is transportation.

check.q: What does a store clerk do?
check.why: A clerk works in the store and puts goods out for people to buy.

check.q: Is a truck driver a worker who helps bread?
check.why: The driver does not make bread, but moving it is a job that helps.

lessons.title: Illinois Farms
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois farms grow a lot of corn and soybeans.
reading: Illinois has many farms. Farmers there grow lots of corn and *soybeans*. Some grow wheat too. Big fields stretch far and wide.
Corn feeds people and farm animals. Soybeans are used to make oil and food. Trucks and trains carry these *crops* all over.
Every farm needs workers. Someone drives the tractor. Someone fixes it. Someone sells the seeds. Every step is a job.

words.d: plants a farmer grows to use or sell
small beans grown on farms, used for food and oil

look.title: A Summer Field
look.text: Picture a summer field in Illinois. Green corn stands taller than your dad. Rows of short soybean plants are next to it. A red tractor hums by.
look.prompt: Name two jobs people do on this farm.

check.q: What do many Illinois farms grow?
check.why: Illinois farms grow a lot of corn and soybeans.

check.q: What is a crop?
check.why: Crops are plants farmers grow to use or sell.

check.q: Who is a worker on a farm?
choices: The person who drives the tractor
check.why: Driving the tractor is a job. The driver is a worker.

lessons.title: You Can Be Both
lessons.mainIdea: You are a consumer every day and a producer sometimes.
reading: You eat, play and learn. You use goods and services. So you are a consumer every day.
You can be a producer too. You draw a card for Grandma. You help rake leaves. You made a good. You gave a service.
Most grown-ups are both. A baker makes bread at work. At home, the baker buys shoes. Everyone uses things. Many people also make things.

words.d: a person who makes goods or gives a service
a person who buys or uses goods and services

look.title: Leo's Saturday
look.text: On Saturday, Leo eats pancakes. Then he helps his neighbor carry bags of groceries. After that, he draws a picture for his aunt.
look.prompt: When is Leo a consumer? When is Leo a producer?

check.q: Leo draws a card for Grandma. What is he?
check.why: Leo made a good, the card. That makes him a producer.

check.q: Leo eats pancakes. What is he?
check.why: Leo uses the pancakes, so he is a consumer.

check.q: Can one person be a producer and a consumer?
check.why: A baker makes bread at work and buys shoes at home. People are often both.

review.q: What is a person who makes goods?
review.why: A producer makes goods or gives services.
A bus ride is a job someone does for you. The others are goods.

review.q: Which step comes right after the mill?
review.why: The mill makes flour. Then the baker uses the flour to bake.

review.q: What carries wheat to the mill?
review.why: Moving goods is transportation. Trucks and trains do it.

review.q: You eat a sandwich. What are you?
review.why: You use the sandwich, so you are a consumer.

review.q: What do many Illinois farms grow?
review.why: Illinois farms grow a lot of corn and soybeans.

chapters.title: A Class Market Day
chapters.bigQuestion: What happens when buyers and sellers meet at a market?

story.title: The Bookmark Table
story.kicker: Room 12 sets up nine tables, and one sells out before recess.
paragraphs: Room 12 had a market day. The class set up nine tables. Kids made cards, bookmarks and paper flowers. Each table had a price sign.
Ana and Sam made bookmarks. They had tassels and bright stars. The sign said "25 cents each" (a class example). Kids lined up fast.
Before recess, every bookmark was gone! Other kids still wanted one. At the card table, only a few cards sold. The card sellers felt puzzled.
After school, the class counted the money. They talked about why the bookmarks sold out. They talked about what to change next time.
story.think: Why do you think the bookmarks sold out? What could the card table try next time?

lessons.title: Buyers and Sellers Meet
lessons.mainIdea: A market is any place where buyers and sellers meet.
reading: A *seller* has something to trade for money. A *buyer* wants to get it. They need a place to meet.
That place is a *market*. A farmers' market is one. A store is one. Room 12's market day is one too.
At a market, buyers look and choose. Sellers show what they have. When both agree, a sale happens.

words.d: a place where buyers and sellers meet to trade
a person who pays money to get something
a person who gives something in trade for money

look.title: Saturday Market
look.text: Look at a farmers' market. Tables hold red tomatoes and yellow corn. A woman hands a bag of peaches to a boy. The boy's mom gives her money.
look.prompt: Who is the seller? Who are the buyers?

check.q: What is a market?
choices: A place where buyers and sellers meet
check.why: A market is any place where buyers and sellers meet to trade.

check.q: Sam gives money for a bookmark. What is Sam?
check.why: Sam pays money to get the bookmark, so Sam is a buyer.

check.q: Which one is a market?
check.why: At a grocery store, buyers and sellers meet. So it is a market.

lessons.title: Setting a Price
lessons.mainIdea: A seller sets a price, and a buyer decides to buy or not.
reading: A *price* is how much money something costs. The seller picks the price. Ana writes "25 cents" on her sign. That is a class example.
The buyer decides. Is the bookmark worth 25 cents to me? If yes, the buyer pays. If no, the buyer walks on.
Two bookmarks at 25 cents each cost 50 cents. 25 plus 25 is 50. The buyer pays 50 cents for both.

words.d: how much money you pay to buy something

look.title: Room 12 Price Signs
look.prompt: Which thing has the lowest price? Which has the highest?

check.q: Who picks the price on the sign?
check.why: The seller writes the price. The buyer then decides.

check.q: Bookmarks are 25 cents each (example). How much for two?
check.why: 25 plus 25 is 50 cents.

check.q: A buyer thinks a card is not worth it. What can the buyer do?
check.why: The buyer decides. A buyer can say no and keep the money.

lessons.title: When Nobody Buys
lessons.mainIdea: If nobody buys, the seller may lower the price.
reading: The card table sells cards for 50 cents each (a class example). Ten minutes go by. Nobody buys a card.
Leo has an idea. He *lowers the price* to 30 cents. Now three kids buy cards! A lower price can bring more buyers.
Sellers watch buyers. When things do not sell, a seller can try a lower price. Or the seller can make the goods better.

words.d: to make something cost less money

look.title: Cards Sold
look.prompt: What happened to cards sold when the price went down?

check.q: No one buys the cards. What might the seller try?
check.why: When nothing sells, a lower price can bring more buyers.

check.q: Leo lowers the price from 50 to 30 cents. How much lower?
check.why: 50 take away 30 is 20 cents.

check.q: Look at the Cards Sold table. At 20 cents, how many sold?
check.why: The table shows 6 cards sold at 20 cents.

lessons.title: When Everyone Wants It
lessons.mainIdea: When many buyers want something, it can sell out.
reading: Ana and Sam made 20 bookmarks. Many more kids wanted one. Soon all 20 were gone. They *sold out*.
When lots of buyers want a thing, it sells fast. Some buyers go home without one. The seller could make more next time.
A seller could also raise the price a little. Then some buyers may choose something else. Sellers watch and learn.

words.d: when a seller has none left because all of it was bought

look.title: The Empty Table
look.text: Picture the bookmark table after ten minutes. The box is empty. Four kids still stand in line. They look sad. Ana and Sam look at each other.
look.prompt: What could Ana and Sam do next market day?

check.q: What does sold out mean?
check.why: Sold out means all of it was bought, so none is left.

check.q: Many kids want bookmarks. What happens?
check.why: When many buyers want something, it sells fast and can sell out.

check.q: Ana made 20 bookmarks and sold 20. How many are left?
check.why: 20 take away 20 is 0. None are left.

lessons.title: Making Things to Sell
lessons.mainIdea: To sell at a market, you first make a product.
reading: Before market day, Room 12 made things. They cut paper. They drew stars. They added string. The things they made are *products*.
Making takes *resources*. Ana used paper, markers and string. She also used her time and her hands.
Good sellers think about buyers. What do my classmates like? Bright colors? Stars? Then they make that.

words.d: a good someone makes to sell
the things and the work used to make something

look.title: The Craft Table
look.text: Look at the craft table. There is a pile of paper, a box of markers and a roll of string. Ana's hands are busy. A stack of bookmarks grows.
look.prompt: What resources is Ana using? Name three.

check.q: Ana makes bookmarks to sell. What are the bookmarks?
check.why: Things you make to sell are products.

check.q: Which is a resource Ana uses?
check.why: Paper is something Ana uses to make the bookmark. It is a resource.

check.q: Why do sellers think about what buyers like?
choices: So buyers will want to buy it
check.why: If you make what buyers like, more buyers will want it.

lessons.title: Counting and Fair Rules
lessons.mainIdea: Fair markets have honest signs, one price for all, and turns.
reading: After market day, Room 12 counted the money. Ana sold 20 bookmarks at 25 cents (class example). 20 times 25 cents is 500 cents. That is $5.
A good market has *fair* rules. Signs tell the truth. Everyone pays the same price. Buyers take turns in line.
Fair rules help everyone. Buyers can trust the sellers. Sellers get buyers who come back. Kind markets work well.

words.d: honest and the same for everyone
coins and bills people use to buy things

look.title: Two Signs
look.text: One table has a sign that says "Big cards." The cards are really tiny. Another table has a sign that says "Small cards, 20 cents." The cards are small.
look.prompt: Which table is fair to buyers? Why?

check.q: Which rule is fair?
check.why: A fair market has one price for everyone.

check.q: Ana sold 4 bookmarks at 25 cents each (example). How much money?
check.why: 25 plus 25 plus 25 plus 25 is 100 cents. That is $1.

check.q: Why should signs tell the truth?
check.why: Honest signs help buyers trust sellers and come back.

review.q: Where do buyers and sellers meet?
review.why: A market is where buyers and sellers meet to trade.

review.q: Who decides to buy or not?
review.why: The seller sets the price. The buyer decides.

review.q: Nobody buys the flowers. What might the seller do?
review.why: A lower price can bring more buyers.

review.q: Everyone wants the bookmarks. What can happen?
review.why: When many buyers want a thing, it can sell out.

review.q: Two cards cost 50 cents each (example). How much for both?

review.why: Taking turns is fair to every buyer.
